content.text: Silvermoon sent its first soldiers to the Horde beneath banners the city had learned to tolerate before it learned to welcome them.

The red field and black device of the Horde hung beside the phoenix standard above the eastern gate. Magisters had warded both against rain, ash, knives, and the small destructive spells favored by people who lacked the courage to throw stones in daylight. Three weeks of proclamations had declared the alliance lawful. Three weeks of arrests had made dissent quieter. Neither effort had made the Horde colors beloved.

Falanaras stood in the departure yard while quartermasters counted thirty-seven sin’dorei into a force assembled to prove a kingdom’s promise. Six Blood Knights wore black plate edged in crimson. Eight Farstriders waited with Lethira beneath oiled cloaks. The magisters had sent four battle-casters and an apprentice whose hands shook whenever he moved beyond the gate wards. Three men and one woman from Murder Row carried narrow blades, lock tools, and the expressions of people invited into respectable service because respectable methods had failed. A warlock named Elthas Emberweave kept his hood raised and his felguard dismissed, though the demon’s contract smoldered against the iron plates sewn into his coat.
Theron checked the straps of his greatshield and looked toward the banner. “It is still hanging.”
“For now,” Lethira said. She tightened her quiver against her hip. “Give the Bazaar another night.”

A mana line had formed across the square behind them. Citizens waited beneath the glow of a public wardstone while armed attendants measured each allotment. Two magisters watched the line from a balcony, their hands folded in sleeves broad enough to hide spellwork.
“They want us gone before someone decides the send-off requires an opinion,” Falanaras said.
“They want us visible while leaving,” Theron replied. “The distinction appears important to government.”

Liadrin walked the files without ceremony. She inspected weapons, armor seals, field dressings, and the governed bonds she could sense without touching. When she reached Falanaras, the captive Light answered her presence through the connection beneath his breastbone. M’uru’s distant anguish entered him as a thin, enduring note.
“You will serve under Gorath Stonebinder,” Liadrin said. “His command is lawful. His suspicion is earned. Give him no cause to regret either.”
“He told me he would test our oath when an enemy offered no honor.”
“Then Hillsbrad has saved him the trouble of waiting.” Her gaze moved to his two-handed sword. “Use what the field requires. When victory gives you a choice, remember what governs the hand.”
“Discipline. Duty. Honor. Remembrance.”
Liadrin inclined her head. “Return with all four.”

They crossed into Lordaeron by Rommath’s transit circle, then marched south beneath a sky heavy with autumn rain. The road left Tirisfal’s dead woods and climbed toward country that still remembered harvest. Hillsbrad’s fields lay brown beneath the season, divided by low walls and streams swollen from the highlands. West across the wet country, Dalaran’s ruin occupied a rise above Lordamere. Broken houses and toppled masonry showed dark around the base of an immense violet dome, opaque beneath the rain; whatever remained at the city’s heart lay hidden behind its magical wall. Human farmsteads stood at long distances from one another. Some flew Southshore blue. Others had black Horde marks painted over doors already broken by war.

Gorath met them at a Forsaken post north of the river. The binding around his ribs was gone, but his left shoulder still moved stiffly from their duel. He carried the same axe and wore small Horde pennants tied beneath the carved stones at his belt.

Three officers waited with him. Jazreth Shadowtide, a lean Darkspear priest, wore bone charms among strips of dark cloth; shadow moved around him in the wrong direction whenever clouds crossed the sun. Mavren Coldwake had once been a broad human man. Death had tightened gray skin over his jaw and left one cheek opened to the teeth. He carried a rectangular shield scarred by axes and a sword with no ornament except old blood in the fuller. Tahu Windtotem stood a head taller than Gorath, his horns wrapped in red cord and his staff hung with feathers damp from travel.

Gorath looked over Silvermoon’s contribution. His attention paused on Elthas’s hood, the rogues, the green light in every sin’dorei face, and finally Falanaras. “You brought every reason my soldiers have to distrust your people.”
“Silvermoon wished to be representative,” Lethira replied.
Jazreth’s tusks framed a quiet laugh. Mavren gave Lethira a long dead stare. “If that was humor, warn me. My face has limited range.”
Tahu studied the Blood Knights with grave patience. “The Light around you is wounded.”
Falanaras could have offered Liadrin’s answer, Rommath’s answer, or Astalor’s. None would change what the tauren sensed. “Yes.”

Gorath heard the admission and moved on. “Tarren Mill has held against raids for months. Southshore sent a larger force yesterday: infantry, archers, magi, and paladins. They took the southern farms and the ridge above the road. We expect the main assault before dusk. Forsaken hold the mill. My company holds the north road. You will reinforce whichever breaks first.”
“Whose command in the field?” Falanaras asked.
“Mine,” Gorath said. “Until I fall. Then Mavren. Then you.” Several orcs behind him objected without words. Gorath turned his head. The objections ended.

They heard Tarren Mill before they saw it. Cannon fire rolled across the hills. A tower bell clanged without rhythm. Smoke climbed behind the ridge, black at its root and gray where the rain worried it apart.
A Forsaken runner came up the road with one arm hanging by sinew. “South wall breached. Abominations engaged east. Living cavalry through the orchard.”

Gorath drew his axe. “No camp. No rest. Mavren, take the Forsaken and rogues through the mill. Tahu, wounded and eastern flank. Jazreth, with me on the road. Rangers take the ridge. Magisters suppress their cannon and casters.” He looked at Theron, then Falanaras. “Blood Knights divide. Shields to the breach. Swords with me.”
The orders cut the unfamiliar force into useful pieces. Whatever distrust remained had to keep pace.
The road descended into battle.

Tarren Mill crouched around a stone tower and timber buildings stained by plague, weather, and Forsaken occupation. The southern palisade had opened inward. Human infantry forced through the gap behind blue shields while skeletal guards and Forsaken axemen fought among burning carts. To the east, an abomination dragged a broken cavalry horse beneath its cleaver as Alliance riders circled beyond reach. Archers held the ridge. Their arrows fell in disciplined flights, driving Horde defenders away from the breach each time they tried to close it.
Gorath struck his axe against the road. Earth rose ahead of the charging company in a rolling shelf. Arrows hit the sudden bank or climbed over it too steeply to retain force. “Now,” he said.

Falanaras passed the earthen cover at a run. Two Blood Knights kept pace, swords kindling red-gold along their edges. Jazreth cast one hand toward the ridge. Darkness unrolled across the archers’ sight, deep enough that the next flight scattered. Horde soldiers roared from the breach.

The first human spearman braced for Falanaras’s charge. He turned the spearhead against his breastplate, let it slide, and cut through the shaft. His return stroke entered beneath the man’s lifted arm. Holy force burst from the wound and threw the body into the shield behind it.
First blood under Horde command soaked the edge of his sword.
There was no revelation in it. The man died with surprise still in his eyes. Falanaras stepped over him because Gorath’s line was advancing and another spear had already found his range.

The Blood Knights hit the infantry with the violence Silvermoon had promised in Undercity. One cast a fan of radiance low across the mud and broke three shield grips at once. Another drove both hands into a wounded orc’s split breastplate; stolen Light sealed the pumping artery before the orc could finish falling. Falanaras kept the greatsword moving. Each impact carried force through wood, steel, and flesh. M’uru’s pain sounded beneath every draw, distant enough to endure and impossible to mistake for consent.
Human soldiers recoiled from the crimson tint.

A paladin behind their line raised his warhammer. Golden light spread through the blue ranks as warmth, steadiness, and the conviction that the ground beneath them could still be held. “Profaners!” he shouted. “The Light bears witness!”
Falanaras felt the paladin’s conviction pass through the human ranks, warming tired limbs and steadying shield arms. He answered by putting his sword through the next shield.

The human line bent without breaking. Their paladins did more than strike. One stood in the breach with a shield lifted while a quiet current of gold strengthened every armored body around him. Another laid a hand against a soldier’s back as he fought, closing a sword wound beneath mail. A third drove the ferrule of his hammer into the churned earth and spoke over it. Gold spread under Horde boots in a shallow field that burned Forsaken flesh and made living muscles seize with sacred heat.
Mavren entered it anyway. Smoke lifted from his greaves. He caught a human shield on his own, hacked the bearer behind the knee, and shouted, “If holiness intends to stop me, it requires better aim.”

Theron’s shield file reached him. A red-gold barrier folded over the Forsaken as the human paladin brought his hammer down. Sacred gold and stolen radiance collided, each making the other look harsher.

Tahu became a bear beside the burning stable. Bone and hide surged outward until his forepaws struck the mud with enough weight to jar the nearby carts. He met the Alliance cavalry where the abomination had failed, taking a lance across one massive shoulder and overturning horse and rider with the same charge. Lethira’s rangers shot past him. Their arrows found reins, exposed throats, and the hands of cavalrymen trying to turn.

A bolt of blue fire descended from the ridge. One of Silvermoon’s magisters caught it against a layered ward. The spell spread across the barrier in branching lines, searching for weakness. Elthas stepped from behind the earthwork and tore open his contract. His felguard arrived in green flame, axe already falling into the Alliance caster’s bodyguard.
Orcs who had distrusted the warlock shouted approval before remembering themselves.

Gorath drove the center forward until a golden hammer of force struck him in the chest and stopped the attack around him. The blow carried no iron. It rang through armor and bone with the authority of a bell. Gorath dropped to one knee, stunned, while an Alliance paladin advanced to finish him.

Falanaras reached the shaman first. He turned the descending warhammer with his crossguard and felt the gold-burning weapon sear through both gauntlets. The paladin stared into his green eyes, then at the red-gold current running along the sword. “What have you done to it?”
“What was required.”

The answer enraged him. At his word, white radiance tightened around the hammerhead. Falanaras caught the next strike on a barrier held close to his body and released the ward outward. The paladin flew back into his own line.
Gorath regained his feet. “You always answer sermons with excessive force?”
“When time permits.”

The Alliance horn sounded twice from the ridge. Their infantry opened lanes through the center. Paladins moved into them in pairs—one shield forward while the other sent compact bolts of gold across the field—and archers shifted fire toward the Blood Knights. The change was deliberate. The humans had identified the threat and placed faith against theft.

One of those bolts struck a Blood Knight before she could raise her guard. Radiance bound her feet to the earth. Three arrows found her breastplate. Theron planted his shield over her, broke the binding with a pulse through the mud, and carried her bodily behind the line.
“Fal!” Lethira called from the slope.
He followed her arrow toward the ridge.

A man in silver-edged plate descended through the human ranks with a warhammer in one hand and a kite shield in the other. Dark hair showed beneath his open helm. The scar across his chin caught the gold burning around him.
Edric Hale saw him at the same moment.

The battlefield narrowed without becoming quieter. Falanaras still heard shields split, wounded men call for water, Jazreth chanting beneath the din, and the abomination bellowing as Tahu knocked a gnome clear across the field. Through all of it came the remembered cadence.
Edric grounded his stance. Drew breath. Spoke a brief invocation. Gave the Light its purpose.

At his brief prayer, warmth settled across Edric’s shoulders. Gold brightened the rim of his shield and the head of his hammer. The soldiers nearest him straightened as his devotion spread among them.
In the Ghostlands, Falanaras had watched that cadence preserve life. Here it prepared Edric to take his.
“Fal,” Edric said. No warmth remained in the name.
“Edric.”
“You chose this.”
Falanaras looked once at the Horde banner above the mill, snapping in smoke. “Yes.”
Edric’s gaze moved over the Blood Knights fighting behind him. “That is the Light.” Horror roughened his voice more than hatred did. “Bound. Hurt. I can hear it in what you wield.”
“You hear enough to condemn. Never enough to help.”
“I came north. I searched for you.”
“After.” The old wound opened with familiar ease. “You all came after.”

An orc lunged between them. Edric’s shield struck the warrior aside without breaking his arm. A human swordsman rushed Falanaras from the opposite direction. Falanaras cut through his breastplate and left him dead in the mud.
Edric watched the body fall. “You call that necessity now?”
“I call it battle.”
“So did every butcher who found a banner.”
Edric raised his hammer. Falanaras brought the greatsword to guard.
Their first collision split the noise around them.
Edric fought as a wall that advanced.

His shield received the greatsword near the forte, where Falanaras had least leverage. His hammer answered in compact blows toward elbow, knee, and helm. He wasted no movement. Gold traveled from his armor into the torn ground, giving his footing a certainty mud should have denied him. Each time Falanaras tried to circle, Edric turned the shield and shortened the available field.

Falanaras fought to open what Edric closed. The two-handed blade threatened from beyond hammer reach, changed level midway through cuts, and made defense expensive even when it succeeded. Red-gold force lengthened the danger beyond the steel. Edric’s shield rang under one strike, flared beneath the next, and held.
They had sparred with wooden swords as boys. Neither had learned this future from the other.
Edric spoke one word. The radiance held close around him compressed above the hammerhead and broke free.

Gold crossed the space between them before Falanaras could evade. It struck his chest, entered the joints of his armor, and locked his stride beneath the demand for justice. Edric followed behind it. His hammer hit the flat of the greatsword, tore the point downward, and drove a second blow into Falanaras’s ribs.
Plate folded. Breath vanished.
Falanaras released a burst from his left hand. Edric raised the shield. Red-gold fire broke around its rim and scorched a furrow through the infantry behind him, but the paladin remained upright.
“Power without grace,” Edric said.
Falanaras forced air back into his lungs. “Grace without arrival.”
He widened the draw from M’uru. Anguish sharpened beneath his heart. The sword ignited from guard to point, and he drove forward hard enough to make Edric yield three steps.
Edric gave ground only until his boot entered the fading circle another paladin had burned into the mud. The gold surged at his presence. Falanaras’s next step landed inside it.

Holy heat climbed through his greaves. It burned Mavren’s dead flesh, Elthas’s fel contract, and Falanaras’s coerced radiance with equal hostility. Edric struck his sword arm. A stunning pulse burst from the hammer and turned every muscle rigid.
Falanaras fell to one knee.
Edric could have crushed his skull. Instead he reversed the hammer and drove the haft against the sword, knocking it from numb fingers. “Yield.”
The same word Falanaras had given Gorath. Here no terms protected either life. An Alliance archer raised his bow beyond Edric. Lethira’s arrow reached the man first.
Falanaras looked up. “You know me better than that.”
“I knew you before you decided survival excused everything.”
“No.” Feeling returned as knives along Falanaras’s arm. “You knew me before survival asked anything of you.”

Falanaras called the sword back with a lash of red-gold force. Edric intercepted it on the shield, but the distraction let Falanaras rise and close inside the hammer’s arc. He struck with gauntlet, shoulder, and the crossguard when the blade returned to his hand. Edric answered with the shield edge beneath his chin.
Blood filled Falanaras’s mouth.
He opened a path between his pulse and the sword.

The change began in his own body. Heat opened along his veins. Each heartbeat fed the edge until crimson ran within the gold. He cut across Edric’s shield. Holy force detonated through both men. The power took payment from Falanaras as it struck; pain tore beneath his ribs, and blood seeped through the folded plate Edric had damaged.
The shield’s upper rim split.
Edric stared at the wound Falanaras had accepted to create his. “You consume yourself and call it strength.”
“We learned from generous teachers.”

Edric’s anger broke his economy. He thrust the damaged shield forward and sent gold snapping from its rim, struck high behind the burst, and let the hammer’s holy charge flare before contact. Falanaras met it with all the force he had been taught never to fear.
Gold and red-gold touched.
The combined flash swallowed a whole section of the battlefield.

Light rose in a column above the road and spread outward at ground level. Human infantry flew across the mud. Orcs tumbled behind Gorath’s earthen bank. Arrows became brief black strokes and vanished. The golden field burned into the mud ruptured in a ring, throwing clods of blazing soil against the mill walls. Windows burst inward. For one immense heartbeat, every shadow from Tarren Mill to the ridge pointed away from two men.
Sound returned as a blow.
Falanaras struck the ground on his back. Edric landed near the broken remains of a cart. Between them, the road had been scoured bare of fighters for thirty paces.
The battle recoiled from the hollow they had made.

On the Horde side, Theron rose behind his shield with smoke curling from its face. Gorath dragged an orc clear of the scorched road. Jazreth’s shadows had collapsed close around him, shielding three wounded soldiers. Lethira stood on the lower slope with her bow drawn and no shot she could safely take.

Across the open ground, Alliance paladins formed a half-circle behind Edric. Their infantry gathered beyond them. No one entered. Residual Light crawled over the road in red and gold, seizing at boots and weapon points. The next soldier who approached would step between forces still seeking release.
The wider battle continued at the edges—at the breach, in the orchard, beneath the ridge—but here both armies watched.
Gorath met Falanaras’s eyes. He offered no order to stop.
Edric stood. Half his shield hung from its straps. He tore it free and let it fall.
Without the shield, Edric changed.

His left hand closed around the hammer beneath the right. He drew one measured breath despite blood running from his ear. Golden radiance gathered close to his armor, repairing what it could: breath steadied, the cut at his brow sealed, and the weakness in his forward leg eased. He did not heal himself completely. He restored what the fight required.

Falanaras pressed his palm to the break in his breastplate. The Light answered without prayer. He pulled it through M’uru’s pain and forced flesh to close beneath bent steel. Relief came sharp, effective, and accompanied by the captive’s fractured song.
Edric heard enough of it to flinch. “That suffering is inside every mercy you give yourself.”
“Yes.” Falanaras lifted his sword.
“How do you bear it?”
“The same way you bear arriving too late. Poorly. While there is work.”
They crossed the emptied road again.

Edric’s two-handed hammer work carried more reach and less shelter. His old habits remained: high guard, direct return, pressure regained after every retreat. Each strike released holy fire gathered close around his weapon. Falanaras answered in broad cuts and violent wards, trying to crush through the cadence.
He failed.

Edric’s Light did not meet force with equal force. Each brief prayer changed one condition of the exchange. Red-gold bands closed around his ankle; gold coursed through his limbs and tore them apart. Falanaras found a killing line; radiance sheathed Edric for one heartbeat, turned the blade, and vanished before the counter. Power gathered around the hammer, discharged across the space between them, then yielded to a fresh invocation. Every prayer created a brief, exact advantage, then made room for the next.
Falanaras possessed more raw power. Edric kept deciding what that power was permitted to accomplish.
A hammer blow broke the ward at Falanaras’s shoulder and numbed his sword hand. Another struck his thigh. Edric pivoted behind the impact and drove him toward the center of the scoured road.
Falanaras drew deeper. The captive Light surged in answer. He could fill the hollow with fire. He could make Edric’s protections irrelevant through abundance and leave neither man standing.
That was how a Blood Knight lost while winning.

Rynel’s voice returned from a practice yard that no longer existed: power was never the point of a spellbreaker’s work. Read the hostile current. Find where intent passed into use. Break the use. Subdue the source.
Falanaras had been fighting as though becoming a Blood Knight had replaced the man trained before it.
Edric grounded his stance.
Breath. Word. Intent.
Falanaras stopped watching the Light and watched the passage into command.
Edric drew breath for a brief prayer before Falanaras cast the binding.

The answer entered through faith, gathered around the paladin’s will, and fixed itself into armor and flesh as a refusal of restraint. Falanaras reached with the part of his training that had once stripped command from necromancers and turned magisterial wards against their makers.
He could not take Edric’s faith. He caught the enchantment built from it.

Falanaras hooked the working at the instant it settled and pulled. Gold tore from Edric’s limbs in long bands. For a breath it wrapped Falanaras instead, burning against the stolen red-gold already inside him. Edric’s eyes widened.
The greatsword swept low. Edric tried to turn with the unnatural ease he had called and found ordinary weight where grace had been. The flat of the blade struck his knee and brought him down.
Falanaras did not follow with the killing edge. He touched two fingers to the radiance fading around Edric’s hammer and drew a bounded measure into himself.
The measured power taken from Edric tasted different from M’uru: mortal, structured, offered to another purpose before Falanaras intercepted it.
Edric recovered with a burst that cast Falanaras back. “You steal even from me.”
“I disrupt enemies. You chose the category.”
Edric rose behind a golden shell.

Radiance closed around him from all sides, without seam or weak face. The enclosure carried a purity Falanaras’s spellbreaker senses could read and could not immediately break. His sword struck it and rebounded. Red-gold force spread uselessly across the sphere. Edric stood within it, head bowed, one hand tightening on the hammer while healing light restored the leg Falanaras had damaged.
Alliance soldiers shouted from beyond the scorched ring. They knew this sign. Some began to advance, expecting their paladin to emerge renewed.
Gorath lifted his axe. Theron braced. Neither crossed into the residual fire.
Falanaras stepped around the shield and studied it. Invulnerability was still a working. A working still required purpose, duration, and an ending.
The shield faded when Edric chose offense.
Falanaras saw the decision travel through him before the gold thinned: heel set, hands shifted, breath gathered for the stunning blow meant to end the fight. He let Edric begin it.
The hammer rose.
Falanaras released the arcane power he had tapped.

Blue-white energy erupted from him in a tight torrent. It carried the hard note of blood elf magic beneath M’uru’s radiance. The burst struck Edric at the opening of his invocation and silenced the word in his throat. Gold guttered along the hammer. The stunning force failed to gather.
Falanaras entered the empty beat.

He turned the hammer past his head with the greatsword’s crossguard, caught Edric’s wrist beneath the quillon, and twisted. Spellbreaker technique took the weapon from a paladin who had expected a contest of holy strength.
The hammer fell.
Falanaras kicked it beyond Edric’s reach.
Edric struck him barehanded across the broken breastplate. Falanaras’s ribs shifted. He answered with the pommel beneath Edric’s jaw. The paladin staggered but remained standing.
Again Falanaras opened his pulse to the sword.
Pain flared through his own wound. Crimson deepened inside the sword’s radiance. At arm’s length, he released everything the blood-fed power had stored in one immediate holy strike.

The blow hit Edric’s breastplate without the blade touching him. Gold burst from every seam. Edric crossed the road and struck the earth on his back, armor smoking. The same release drove blood from beneath Falanaras’s cuirass and nearly took his legs with it.
Both men tried to rise.

Falanaras reached his feet first because blood elf training had taught him to fight while hungry, because Liadrin had taught him to accept the cost he chose, and because Rynel had taught him that the decisive point often appeared after strength was spent.
Edric made one knee. The other would not hold.
Falanaras crossed the final distance.

Edric’s hammer lay behind him. The golden shell he had raised was spent. The soldiers of both armies watched from the edges of the blasted ground. The Alliance line had begun to buckle elsewhere; Tahu and the abomination were gone from the orchard, and Horde banners moved along the ridge. None of that changed the exposed throat above Edric’s gorget.
Falanaras set the greatsword’s point against it.
Edric looked up through blood and sacred smoke. “Do it.”
“No.”
“Do not make your corruption into pity.”
“The fight is decided.”
“We are enemies.”
“Yes.” Falanaras held the sword entirely still. “That does not grant me every use of victory.”
Edric’s face tightened. Mercy reached him as humiliation because hatred had left no gentler place for it to land. “You think this proves honor?”
“No,” Falanaras said. “It keeps my oath.”
An Alliance horn sounded from the ridge: three descending notes. Withdrawal.

Falanaras lowered the sword enough for Edric to breathe without steel against his skin. He did not offer a hand. Edric would have refused it, and some wounds did not improve when displayed before armies.
Human paladins entered the ring cautiously. One kept his shield toward Falanaras while another pulled Edric upright. Their gold recoiled from the red-gold fire still moving across Falanaras’s armor.
Beyond them, among the withdrawing Alliance, a high elf stood beneath a blue cloak.

Caelir had no weapon raised. Rain had darkened his pale hair. He watched Falanaras across the ruined road with grief stripped of every defense, and beneath it lay shame—whether for his brother, for the Alliance defeat, or for his own place among those leaving, Falanaras could not know.
Neither brother moved.
Caelir reached Edric’s side and took part of his weight. Only then did Falanaras understand that he had been close enough to intervene and had chosen witness instead.
Edric followed Falanaras’s gaze and saw Caelir. Something passed between the two men. Then Edric looked back. “At the way station, you told me to carry both truths. I tried.”
“So did I.”
“You chained one of them.”
The answer existed beneath Silvermoon in a magisterial cage. It sang through Falanaras’s blood while the wounds it had closed continued to ache. “Yes.”
Edric had wanted denial. Falanaras saw it in the fresh anger that entered his face. Denial would have made the enemy simpler.

Caelir turned him toward the ridge. The human retreat gathered around them in disciplined groups, paladins holding the rear beneath overlapping shields. Falanaras watched until rain and soldiers took his brother from sight.
No reconciliation followed the spared life. Mercy had preserved the possibility of another meeting and guaranteed nothing about what either man would bring to it.
Tarren Mill remained Horde-held when darkness came.

The victory smelled of wet ash, opened bodies, alchemical stores, and the sweet rot of the Forsaken buildings. Southshore’s force left more than eighty dead across the ridge and road. Horde losses filled the mill’s storehouse after the grain was thrown into the rain. Tahu moved among the wounded in his own body again, setting splints with hands broad enough to cover a human chest. Jazreth drew pain from a dying troll and took some of it into the shadows around himself. Blood Knights healed orcs who had flinched from them that morning. Forsaken accepted the same radiance without comment, smoke rising where it touched dead flesh.
The battlefield had answered every political argument with work and left the moral ones alive.

Theron found Falanaras seated against the mill wall while an apprentice cut away the folded section of his breastplate. His own shield had lost most of its black lacquer. Lethira stood beside him with an arrow still nocked, as if the Alliance might reconsider after dark.
“You cleared adequate room,” she said.
“The road was crowded.”
“I had a shot before the flash.”
“At Edric?”
“At his knee.” Her expression told him the distinction mattered. “Then you turned the hillside into the sun and spoiled it.”
Theron lowered himself carefully beside Falanaras. “For accuracy, it resembled two suns making a poor decision.”
The apprentice looked between them, uncertain whether laughter was permitted near so much blood. Falanaras gave him permission by attempting it first. The effort hurt too badly to succeed.

Gorath approached after the apprentice finished binding Falanaras’s ribs. The shaman had blood dried along one tusk and a new cut across the hides at his shoulder. “You defeated the paladin with the training you carried before your order.”
“With all of it.”
“I saw you tear that prayer’s answer from him.”
“Briefly.”
“And silence his prayer.” Gorath’s suspicion had not vanished. It had acquired detail. “Your people collect dangerous answers.”
“We ran out of safe ones.”

Gorath looked toward the scoured road, where rain hissed against the last pockets of holy fire. “In the Undercity, witnesses and agreed terms told you where honor required you to stop. Today your enemy asked you to kill him.”
“He was beaten.”
“You stopped anyway.”
“The oath was mine. His hatred could not release me from it.”
Gorath grunted. “Then I have seen what I asked to see.”
Mavren came to report that the southern breach could be closed before morning. One arm had been severed below the elbow. He carried it under the other as casually as a misplaced tool.

“The elf rogues reached the cannon,” he told Gorath. “The warlock’s demon ate a horse. The magisters objected to the mill’s warding and improved it without invitation. Your representative force remains irritating.”
“Any complaints about the Blood Knights?” Gorath asked.
Mavren looked at Falanaras. “Their healing burns.”
“You are dead,” Theron said.
“I had noticed. The burning remains inconvenient.” He shifted the severed arm. “They held the field.”
From Mavren, it carried the weight of praise.

Gorath assigned watches without regard for nation. Orcs took the wall beside rangers. Murder Row’s scouts went south with Forsaken who could travel without breath or complaint. Tahu slept near the wounded. Jazreth stood the first ritual watch over the dead of four peoples.
Falanaras climbed the tower before dawn.

The battlefield lay gray beneath retreating rain. Horde burial crews moved among the road and ridge. Far to the south, covered Alliance lanterns marked the withdrawal toward Southshore. One of those lights might belong to Edric. Another might fall across Caelir’s face while he decided what report to send Dalaran about the brother he had found alive again.

Below, the Horde banner flew over Tarren Mill. The phoenix standard hung beside it, smoke-stained and torn along one edge. During the night someone had tied the two poles together so the wind would not bring either down. The knot was ugly but held.

Silvermoon had answered its first call. Blood elf power had preserved orc, troll, tauren, and Forsaken lives. Their lives had preserved his people in return. Belonging remained too generous a word for what existed among them.
Service was enough for the morning.
He rested one hand against the bandage beneath his armor and felt M’uru through the bond.

The naaru’s pain had accompanied every wound he closed, every barrier he raised, every strike he drove into Edric’s defenses. Victory had made the source no less captive. Mercy had made Falanaras no less responsible for what he carried. Honor could govern the hand. It could not absolve the power inside it.

From the yard below came Gorath’s voice ordering the morning patrol. Theron answered. Lethira complained about the hour. Mavren demanded someone with two hands help fasten his severed arm before it stiffened in the wrong position.
Falanaras turned from the southern lights and descended to join them.
He had shed first blood for the Horde. The next war was already gathering beyond the horizon, and now there were soldiers beneath its banner who knew exactly what kind of weapon Silvermoon had sent.
